newsitem.title: USA: Key senators support U.S. aid for Egypt.
newsitem.headline: Key senators support U.S. aid for Egypt.

text.p: An influential Republican senator said on Tuesday he will seek to restore specified funding of $2.1 billion in aid to Egypt in next year's foreign aid package when it comes before the full U.S. Senate next month.

Senate Appropriations Committee Chairman Ted Stevens of Alaska joined with several other committee members and the Clinton administration to support continuing to earmark annual military and economic assistance for Egypt in return for its backing of the Middle East peace process.

Stevens said he will bring the issue before the full Senate as an amendment to the 1998 foreign aid budget. This year's budget of $13.2 billion is an increase of almost $800 million over the 1997 funding.

The senior Democrat on the panel, Sen. Robert Byrd of West Virginia, and the senior Democrat on the Foreign Operations Subcommittee, Sen. Patrick Leahy of Vermont, vowed strong support for the funding, called a set-aside, of the full $3.0 billion for Egypt.

An earmark simply specifies in law the funding that will go to Cairo in the year starting Oct. 1. Even without an earmark the White House would be free to provide the aid from the U.S. foreign aid budget.

Money has been set aside each year for Egypt and Israel in return for their continued involvement in the peace process that began with the Camp David negotiations in 1978. As usual, the foreign aid bill earmarked $3.0 billion for Israel.

Foreign Operations Subcommitee Chairman Sen. Mitch McConnell surprised the Senate last week with his proposal to end the traditional set-aside for Cairo and add a new earmark of $250 million for Jordan.

McConnell, a Kentucky Republican, promised several hours of debate on the issue before the full Senate. His efforts were aimed, he said, at sending a direct and clear signal that Egypt should "play a consistent role" in the peace process.

During the committee discussion he cited Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak's "troubling" ties to Libya, a country on the U.S. list of states that support terrorism, and leveled heavy criticism of his efforts to further peace in the Middle East.
In defence of Egypt, Democratic Sen. Patrick Leahy of Vermont noted Egypt's early support for Middle East peace.
"Egyptians for a long, long time were in a very lonely place in the Arab world," Leahy said.
McConnell noted that the United States has provided Egypt with more than $42 billion to further the Middle East peace process. Israel has received $59 billion.
